meaning: Navel (of the earth); the stone at Delphi regarded as the centre of the world

phonemes.desc: Short omicron with the labial nasal m — a closed, rounded opening.
Aspirated phi (an aspirated p in the classical language) plus alpha and lambda.
The final syllable bearing the acute: short omicron under stress at the word's end, as ὀμφαλός requires.

pronunciation.approximation: 'om-fah-LOSS' — the accent falls on the last syllable; classical phi is an aspirated p, not the modern f.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ὀμφαλός (omphalós), 'navel' — of a body, and by extension the navel of the earth

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ὀμφή (omphḗ), 'divine voice, oracle' — an ancient and tempting association with Delphi, though the derivation is uncertain

kin.label: Pre-Greek
kin.form: Beekes judges ὀμφαλός a Pre-Greek word — fitting for an object that belongs to Delphi's oldest strata

pronunciation.note: Omphalós is Tier 2: the restoration preserves exactly one feature ASCII loses — the final acute accent marking stress. There is no long vowel (η/ω) and no circumflex, so the name stands at Tier 2.

domains.title: Navel
domains.subtitle: Navel, Center, Delphi
domains.lead: The omphalós was the stone at Delphi regarded as the navel — the exact center — of the world. Set in the innermost sanctuary, wrapped in a woolen net and flanked by golden eagles, it was not an image of a god but a marker of where the world's middle lay, and the Pythia prophesied beside it.

cards.name: The Stone at Delphi
cards.desc: A rounded Hymettian-marble boss, carved with a net pattern, that stood in the adyton where the Pythia gave her oracles (Pausanias 10.16.3).

cards.name: The Navel of the Earth
cards.desc: Zeus released two eagles from the ends of the world; where they met, at Delphi, the stone marked the center of all lands (Strabo 9.3.6).

cards.name: The Swaddled Stone
cards.desc: The stone Kronos swallowed in place of the infant Zeus was, in the later tradition, set up at Delphi as a wonder and a sign (Hesiod, Theogony 485–497; Pausanias 10.24.6).

cards.name: The Seat of Prophecy
cards.desc: Apollo's oracle spoke beside the stone, in the sanctuary where the god had struck down the serpent Python (Homeric Hymn to Apollo 300ff.).

symbols.name: The net-covered stone
symbols.meaning: The omphalos itself, wrapped in the woolen agrenon net that veiled the world's center (Pausanias 10.16.3)

symbols.name: The two golden eagles
symbols.meaning: Zeus's birds, set one on either side of the stone as witnesses to the center-finding

symbols.name: The navel of a newborn
symbols.meaning: The body's own center — ὀμφαλός is the infant's navel, the mark where nourishment once entered

symbols.name: The cleft of Delphi
symbols.meaning: The rock fissure beneath the temple where Apollo's arrows struck Python and the prophetic power rose

mythology.lead: The omphalós has no biography because it is a place made stone: the story of Delphi's navel is the story of how the Greeks decided where the middle of the world was — by eagle, by oracle, and by the stone that stood for the infant god.

myths.title: The Eagles of Zeus
myths.text: In the story told at Delphi, Zeus wished to know where the exact center of the earth lay. He released two eagles — some say from the eastern and western edges of the world — and bade them fly toward each other; they met above Delphi, and where they met the god fixed the omphalós, the navel-stone. The tale is preserved in the geographical tradition that culminates in Strabo (9.3.6), who repeats it as the sanctuary's own account of itself. The myth is a cartography in miniature: instead of measuring the world, the Greeks let two birds draw its diagonals and set a stone where the lines crossed. Delphi did not claim to be everywhere; it claimed to be the middle — the one point from which the whole could be surveyed, and the one point, therefore, where a god might conveniently speak to all mortals at once. Every subsequent oracle of the sanctuary traded on this founding geometry.

myths.title: The Stone in the Innermost Room
myths.text: Pausanias (10.16.3) describes what the visitor could actually see: in the innermost sanctuary of Apollo's temple, the adyton, lay the omphalos, covered — the Delphians said — with the net thrown over it, with two golden eagles standing upon it. Beside it, in the same most-holy space, stood the tripod on which the Pythia mounted to give her responses, and the ever-burning hearth of the sanctuary. The stone was thus not a cult statue but a boundary-marker of the cosmos, kept in the room where heaven and earth touched. Its material facts are modest — a carved marble boss a little over a meter high — but its placement was the whole argument: the center of the world was a place you could stand next to, touch, and consult. Pausanias's description is the one fixed point on which the identification of the surviving stone rests.

myths.title: What Kronos Swallowed
myths.text: Hesiod (Theogony 485–497) tells how Rhea, pregnant with Zeus, asked her parents Gaia and Ouranos to save the child from Kronos, who devoured each of his newborns. They gave her a great stone wrapped in swaddling clothes; Kronos 'seized it in his hands and thrust it down into his belly, the wretch, nor did he know in his heart that in place of his son his invincible, unshaken stone was left.' The later tradition — reported at Delphi itself and recorded by Pausanias (10.24.6) — identified this very stone with the omphalos at Delphi. The world's center thus conceals a substitution: where a god should have been destroyed, a stone was swallowed instead, and Zeus lived to overthrow his father. The navel of the earth is also the stone of rescue — the dummy that fooled Time and made the present order of the cosmos possible.

myths.title: Apollo, Python, and the Chasm
myths.text: The Homeric Hymn to Apollo (300ff.) tells how the young god came to the rocky cleft at Delphi, where a spring flowed and a she-dragon, Python, lay — 'there the son of Leto with his mighty bow slew the bloated, mighty beast.' The dragon's name gave the place its older name, Pytho, and the goddess who had held the oracle there yielded it to him. On the foundation of Apollo's temple the omphalos stood beside the very chasm from which — in the later tradition reported by the sources — the prophetic power rose to the Pythia enthroned above it. The myth makes the center of the world a conquered place: the middle is not given but won by an arrow, and the stone that marks it stands where a dragon's breath once rose. Delphi's claim to centrality is thus also a claim of legitimacy — the oracle speaks from the exact spot where the god's victory made speech divine.

lore.syncretism: Rome built its own navel: the Umbilicus Urbis Romae, a travertine marker in the Roman Forum, where the symbolic center of the empire was ritually defined, its rounded form echoing the Delphic original. In late antiquity and the Middle Ages the idea of a world-navel multiplied — Jerusalem, Constantinople, even Glastonbury in English legend each claimed a central, omphalic status — proof that the Greek idea had become a portable form of pride. The English language keeps the word as a learned synonym for the center of anything, and the modern mockery of self-absorption as 'navel-gazing' (omphaloskepsis) returns the word to its first, bodily meaning. The stone at Delphi thus survived its own religion: a pagan center-marker became the West's standing metaphor for wherever people believe the world's meaning is concentrated.
lore.culturalLegacy: Delphi's omphalos made 'center' a claim any city could dream of. Roman emperors consulted the oracle and copied the stone; medieval mapmakers drew Jerusalem at the world's middle; and the modern phrase 'navel-gazing' preserves the Greek word in everyday speech. The archaeological site of Delphi, a UNESCO World Heritage site, still draws travelers to the temple foundations where the adyton — and the stone — once stood. In psychology, the Delphic 'know thyself' has been read together with the omphalos as an emblem of the inward journey to the center of the self, a reading popularized by Jung's school. The word also lives quietly in anatomy, where the umbilicus keeps the Greek root in every newborn's first scar. Few small stones have spread so far: a marble boss from a mountain sanctuary became the template for every claim, sacred or secular, to be the middle of things.
lore.extendedMeditation: Every culture draws its maps with a center. The Hebrews had Zion; the Romans had the Umbilicus; the medieval world chose Jerusalem; the modern mind, told there is no privileged point in space, has relocated the center inward. The omphalos is the Greek form of this universal habit — a stone that says: here, and not elsewhere, is where the world is anchored. What is remarkable about Delphi's version is its modesty. The center was not a throne or a temple tower but a carved marble lump, veiled in a fisherman's net and guarded by two eagles. The message seems to be that the middle of things is not a summit to be conquered but a place to be marked and then consulted — a still point, not a peak. Perhaps that is why the image survives: in an age of competing centers and vanishing middles, the omphalos reminds us that a center is something a community agrees upon, sets a stone upon, and returns to when it needs to ask where it is.

sources.name: Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek, s.v. ὀμφαλός

lore.archaeology: The omphalos survives in the Delphi Archaeological Museum: a Hymettian-marble boss carved with a net pattern, a little over a meter high, found in the temple precinct and conventionally identified with the stone Pausanias saw in the adyton. The temple of Apollo — its fourth, stone, phase — still shows the foundations of the inner sanctuary where the stone and the Pythia's tripod stood. The form appears on imperial-period coins of Delphi, always with the net pattern and flanking eagles, and Roman copies of the omphalos type are known from the city of Rome itself. No inscription names the stone; its identification rests on the match between Pausanias's description and the carved marble found on site.
